sections.h2: Where is Randolph, Massachusetts, and what kind of place is it?
sections.html:
Randolph is a suburban city of about 35,000 people in Norfolk County, south of Boston, and it borders Quincy to the north. Its 2020 census count was 34,984, and the land area is 10.1 square miles with very little water.

The Cochato River and the Blue Hill River drain the town into the Neponset River. Elevation is about 184 feet, well above Quincy's 30 feet, and Randolph has almost no harbor frontage, with water making up only about 4 percent of its area.

One quirk: Randolph runs under a city form of government but kept "Town of Randolph" as its official name, one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities that did so. You will see both forms on documents.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Randolph's houses?
sections.html:
Randolph was set off from Braintree in 1793 as a separate town and named for Peyton Randolph, first president of the Continental Congress. Shoe and boot making became its main industry, and by 1850 it ranked among the nation's leading boot producers.

When the shoe trade faded in the early 1900s, the town turned into a residential community, with light manufacturing and services replacing the factories. Population jumped from 9,982 in 1950 to 18,900 in 1960 and 27,035 in 1970, according to the census counts on Wikipedia.

The town's population nearly tripled in two decades. That surge suggests a large share of Randolph's housing went up in a short window, so houses of similar age may need roofs, boilers and windows replaced around the same time. A seller can check each house's age on the assessor's property card.

sections.h2: How do you get around from Randolph?
sections.html:
Randolph sits at a crossroads of major routes, which is a real selling point for commuters. The state and federal roads listed for the town are:

  • Interstate 93 and U.S. Route 1
  • Massachusetts Route 24, the Fall River Expressway
  • Route 28 and Route 139

Rail service comes from the Holbrook/Randolph station on the MBTA Commuter Rail's Fall River/New Bedford Line, and bus service is run by the MBTA and the Brockton Area Transit Authority.

When you describe a Randolph house to a buyer, give drive time to the highway ramps and the rail station. For commuters that detail often matters as much as the kitchen.

sections.h2: Who governs Randolph and where do you take tax questions?
sections.html:
Since the 2009 charter took effect in 2010, Randolph has a council-manager government. Before that, it used representative town meeting, adopted in 1947 and in force from 1949.

Property assessment questions go to the Board of Assessors at Town Hall, 41 South Main Street, Randolph, MA 02368. The town's assessors page says the board meets on the first Thursday of each month at 5:15 p.m. in the Washington Room, and it lists Janet Teal as Principal Assessor.

We did not find a single town page stating the current bill due dates, so confirm your installment dates on the actual tax bill or with the office before you rely on a date.

sections.h2: How does a tax abatement work if you own a house in Randolph?
sections.html:
An abatement is a reduction in your property tax, granted when you can show your home's fair cash value is below its assessed value. The process is set by state law, and the Appellate Tax Board's guide spells out the steps.

  • Pay each installment on time. Late payment can cost you the right to appeal.
  • File the state's approved abatement form with the assessors by the first installment due date on your bill.
  • Assessors have three months to decide. If they do nothing, the request is treated as denied.
  • You then have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

The board values property as of January 1 before the fiscal year. Comparable sales of similar houses nearby are the main evidence. Read the full Appellate Tax Board guide before filing.

sections.h2: What do you need to finish a Randolph house sale?
sections.html:
Randolph is in Norfolk County, so the same registry handles your deed as handles Quincy's. Three items come up on nearly every sale.

  • Fire department certificate. The state requires a seller to show a certificate of compliance that the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet sale standards. The Randolph fire department does the inspection and charges a fee. We did not open a Randolph-specific page, so call the department for its schedule and price.
  • Deed excise. The Norfolk Registry of Deeds collects $2.28 per $500 of consideration at recording, paid by attorney's or bank check.
  • Recording fee. The registry lists $156.00 to record a deed on recorded land.

For a house priced at $400,000, the excise at that rate works out to $1,824.00 (800 units of $500 times $2.28). Your attorney will confirm the exact figure and who pays it under your contract.

Sources: Mass.gov alarm inspection page and the Norfolk Registry fee schedule.

sections.h2: How does the weather around Randolph affect a house sale?
sections.html:
Randolph shares the Blue Hill climate record with neighboring Quincy. Averages there are 53.86 inches of precipitation and 69.7 inches of snow a year, and January lows average 18.3 degrees Fahrenheit.

The record low on that station is minus 21 degrees, and the record high is 101. Houses here carry real heating load in winter and real humidity in summer, so buyers check insulation, the furnace and the roof.

Two rivers drain the town, so ask the town and your insurer whether your lot has any flood exposure. We did not find a Randolph page on flood mapping to cite, so this page makes no claim either way.

sections.h2: What local landmarks and institutions come with Randolph?
sections.html:
Randolph's National Register of Historic Places listings include the Jonathan Belcher House, built in 1806, Stetson Hall, built in 1842, the Appalachian Mountain Club's Ponkapoag Camp and the Gills Farm Archaeological District. The Turner Free Library, opened in 1875, serves as the public library and belongs to the Old Colony Library Network.

The town also has an unusual bit of public-health history. The national Great American Smokeout grew out of a 1969 conversation with a Randolph High School guidance counselor, and the Randolph High class of 1970 organized a local quit-for-a-day event that went national in 1977.

For a seller these are small selling points, but a listing that mentions the library, the schools and the rail station gives a buyer from outside the area a picture of daily life.

sections.h2: What options does a Randolph seller have?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or sell to a cash buyer. Each path trades time and effort against price and certainty.

  • Listing: usually the widest buyer pool, with showings, possible repair requests after inspection and a financing contingency.
  • Selling on your own: you save a commission but handle marketing, paperwork and buyer screening.
  • Cash sale: a faster, simpler close, with a price that can come in below a fully prepared listing.

With so many Randolph houses of the same era, a house that has not been updated may compete against freshly renovated ones. That gap is where an as-is sale tends to make sense.

faqs.q: What county is Randolph, MA in?
faqs.a: Randolph is in Norfolk County, so deeds are recorded at the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds.

faqs.q: Is Randolph a town or a city?
faqs.a: Both, in a sense. It adopted a city charter effective January 2010 with a council-manager government but kept "Town of Randolph" as its official name.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Randolph property assessment?
faqs.a: Contact the Board of Assessors at Town Hall, 41 South Main Street. The board meets the first Thursday of each month at 5:15 p.m.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Randolph?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your alarms meet the standards for a sale.

faqs.q: How much is the Norfolk County deed excise tax?
faqs.a: It is $2.28 for each $500 of the price stated on the deed, according to the Norfolk Registry of Deeds.
